summary: The interview component runs a pre-task structured questionnaire that scopes the work before the agent loop starts. run_interview asks language, framework, project type, testing preference, output location, and scope questions (analyze_task heuristics and detect_existing_project pre-fill defaults), collects answers into an InterviewSession, converts them to a validated InterviewContext, and serializes them via to_system_prompt_section into the agent's system prompt. On the loop it is a boundary 'perceive'/'control' node: it perceives operator intent up front and constrains the loop's plan and budget before the first Planning transition, and it is skippable at any point via Esc.
context_basis: Recommendations were formed by reading src/interview.rs in the context of the full engine's ~600k-token budget framing, so each move treats the interview as a cheap pre-loop scoping pass that shrinks the plan's search space and constrains budget before any tokens are spent iterating.

examples.title: Scope the task before the loop starts
examples.intent: Capture operator intent as structured context so the first plan is grounded, not guessed.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: run_interview runs before the Planning transition and produces an InterviewContext; the loop enters its first iteration already knowing language, scope, and constraints instead of inferring them from the raw task string.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Tap the interview node at the loop's entrance to begin the pre-task questionnaire.
touch_interaction.visual: The node sits as a gate before the Planning node, glowing amber until answered, then green as context is committed.

examples.mini_scenario: Before planning, the interview asks six questions; the answers become the InterviewContext the planner reads on iteration one.
examples.pitfall: The interview must run before the first plan — asking mid-loop wastes the scoping value, since the plan is already committed.

examples.title: Analyze the task to pre-fill defaults
examples.intent: Reduce operator effort by inferring likely answers from the task text.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: analyze_task returns TaskHints (suggests_web_api, suggests_cli, mentioned_languages, ...); the loop pre-selects defaults so fewer questions need answering, tightening scope faster.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press a question node to see the TaskHints that pre-selected its default.
touch_interaction.visual: The inferred default option is pre-highlighted with a small 'from task' badge explaining the guess.

examples.mini_scenario: The task says 'build a REST API in Rust'; analyze_task flags suggests_web_api and mentions Rust, pre-filling both questions.
examples.pitfall: Heuristics are hints, not answers — always let the operator override the pre-fill; a wrong guess silently mis-scopes the loop.

examples.title: Skip language when the project is known
examples.intent: Avoid asking what the environment already answers.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: detect_existing_project inspects for Cargo.toml, package.json, pyproject.toml, or go.mod; when a language is detected the language question is skipped, so the loop scopes without redundant prompting.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Flick past the language question node when the detected project auto-answers it.
touch_interaction.visual: The language node renders pre-filled and dimmed with a 'detected: Rust' chip, non-interactive.

examples.mini_scenario: The cwd holds Cargo.toml; the interview detects Rust, skips the language question, and moves straight to framework.
examples.pitfall: Detection keys on marker files — an unusual layout without them still prompts, so don't assume detection always fires.

examples.title: Offer language-aware framework choices
examples.intent: Present only frameworks that fit the chosen language.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: The framework question's QuestionOptions depend on the selected language (axum/actix/tokio for Rust, FastAPI/Flask/Django for Python, ...); the loop's plan inherits a coherent language+framework pair.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Spread the framework node to fan out the options valid for the selected language.
touch_interaction.visual: Only language-compatible framework chips appear; incompatible ones are absent rather than greyed.

examples.mini_scenario: Language is Python, so the framework question offers FastAPI, Flask, and Django rather than Rust web frameworks.
examples.pitfall: Don't offer cross-language frameworks — an axum option under Python would let the operator scope an impossible plan.

examples.title: Classify the project type
examples.intent: Fix the shape of the deliverable so the plan targets the right structure.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: The project-type question maps to the ProjectType enum (CliTool, WebApi, FrontendUi, Library, FullStack, Script, Other); the loop plans a CLI scaffold vs a web service based on this single choice.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Tap a project-type chip to lock the deliverable shape for the loop.
touch_interaction.visual: Selected type highlights and stamps a type icon (terminal, globe, book) on the interview node.

examples.mini_scenario: The operator picks WebApi; the plan scaffolds routes and handlers rather than a library crate.
examples.pitfall: ProjectType::Other(String) carries a freeform label — the plan must read the string, not assume a built-in variant.

examples.title: Choose a testing discipline
examples.intent: Decide up front how much the loop's verify stage will invest in tests.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: The testing question maps to TestingPreference (Tdd, TestsAfter, Minimal, None); this sets how aggressively the loop's verify stage writes and runs tests each iteration.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Drag the testing dial from None through Minimal, TestsAfter, to Tdd to set verify intensity.
touch_interaction.visual: A four-notch dial; the verify node downstream brightens as the notch climbs toward Tdd.

examples.mini_scenario: The operator selects Tdd; the loop writes a failing test before each implementation act throughout the run.
examples.pitfall: TestingPreference::None means the verify stage skips test authoring — don't silently add tests the operator opted out of.

examples.title: Bound expected effort with scope
examples.intent: Anchor the loop's budget expectation to a size class before it starts iterating.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: The scope question maps to ProjectScope (Quick <100, Small 100-500, Medium 500-2000, Large 2000+ lines); the loop uses this to right-size its budget and iteration count expectations.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Pinch the scope node to compress or expand the expected line-count band.
touch_interaction.visual: A size gauge spans Quick to Large; the loop's budget ring resizes to match the chosen band.

examples.mini_scenario: The operator picks Small; the loop expects a 100-500 line deliverable and sizes its budget for a short run.
examples.pitfall: Scope is an expectation, not a hard cap — don't let the loop refuse legitimate work that overruns the estimated band.

examples.title: Ask a freeform sub-question for output location
examples.intent: Capture a custom subdirectory when the operator wants a new location.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: Selecting 'new subdirectory' triggers ask_freeform to collect the path; the loop's file-writing acts are then scoped to that directory instead of the cwd.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Double-tap the 'new subdirectory' option to open its freeform text field on the canvas.
touch_interaction.visual: A text input slides out beneath the option; the entered path appears as a scoped-directory chip.

examples.mini_scenario: The operator chooses a new subdir and types 'service/'; the loop writes all generated files under service/.
examples.pitfall: The output-location question is skipped inside an existing project — don't force a new-dir prompt when work belongs in place.

examples.title: Serialize answers into the system prompt
examples.intent: Deliver the scoped context to the loop in the form it actually reads.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: to_system_prompt_section formats the InterviewContext as a '## Interview Context (user-specified preferences)' markdown block injected into the agent's system prompt, so every iteration sees the constraints.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Draw a connection from the interview node into the system-prompt node to inject the context block.
touch_interaction.visual: A context ribbon flows along the edge and docks as a labeled section inside the prompt node.

examples.mini_scenario: The context serializes to a markdown section listing Rust, axum, WebApi, Tdd; the planner reads it on every turn.
examples.pitfall: Inject the section once, before the loop — regenerating it mid-run risks contradicting decisions the loop already made.

examples.title: Detect an empty interview and fall back to defaults
examples.intent: Let the loop proceed on best judgment when the operator answered nothing.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: is_empty checks whether every field is None/empty; if the operator skipped everything, the caller omits the context section and the loop plans on its own defaults rather than an empty scaffold.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Flick past the entire interview to skip it; the node collapses to a 'defaults' marker.
touch_interaction.visual: The interview node greys out with an 'empty — using best judgment' badge, and no context edge is drawn.

examples.mini_scenario: The operator hits Esc at the first question; is_empty is true, no section is injected, and the loop uses its own defaults.
examples.pitfall: An empty context is valid — don't inject a blank interview section, which would tell the loop the operator wants nothing rather than left it open.

examples.title: Skip the whole interview with Esc
examples.intent: Give the operator an instant escape from scoping.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: read_line_or_esc detects Esc in TTY mode and returns LineInput::Esc; pressing it at any question stops the questionnaire and returns whatever was collected, so the loop starts immediately.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Flick down anywhere on the questionnaire to abort remaining questions.
touch_interaction.visual: Remaining question nodes fade and the loop's Planning gate unlocks immediately.

examples.mini_scenario: After answering language and framework, the operator hits Esc; those two answers persist and the loop begins.
examples.pitfall: Esc keeps partial answers, it doesn't discard them — don't treat a mid-interview Esc as an empty context.

examples.title: Present numbered multiple-choice questions
examples.intent: Collect an unambiguous answer via a keyed menu.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: ask_multiple_choice renders QuestionOptions with char keys and reads a TTY-aware selection, returning None on Esc or the chosen label; the loop receives a clean enum-mappable answer rather than free text.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Tap a numbered option chip to select it.
touch_interaction.visual: Each option is a keyed chip (a, b, c); the tapped chip fills solid and the rest dim.

examples.mini_scenario: The scope question shows keys a-d; the operator taps 'b' for Small and ask_multiple_choice returns its label.
examples.pitfall: A None return means skipped, not a default choice — the caller must distinguish 'no answer' from 'first option'.

examples.title: Handle non-interactive input gracefully
examples.intent: Keep the interview working when stdin is piped, not a terminal.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: read_line_or_esc falls back to a plain read_line in non-interactive mode (no crossterm raw mode); the loop can still be scoped from a script without a TTY, or cleanly skip.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press the interview node to see whether it's in interactive or piped-input mode.
touch_interaction.visual: A mode badge shows a keyboard glyph for TTY or a pipe glyph for scripted input.

examples.mini_scenario: A CI job pipes answers into selfware init; the fallback read_line consumes them line by line without raw-mode.
examples.pitfall: Esc detection needs raw TTY mode — in piped mode there's no Esc, so scripts must supply explicit skip lines instead.

examples.title: Map answers into typed enums
examples.intent: Turn free labels into the domain enums the loop reasons over.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: parse_project_type, parse_testing_preference, and parse_scope convert selected labels into ProjectType/TestingPreference/ProjectScope; the loop reasons over typed values, not strings.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Double-tap an answered question to see its label resolve into a typed enum value.
touch_interaction.visual: The label chip morphs into a typed badge (e.g. 'Web API' -> ProjectType::WebApi).

examples.mini_scenario: The 'Full TDD' label parses to TestingPreference::Tdd, which the verify stage reads directly.
examples.pitfall: An unrecognized custom label falls through to Other(String) — the loop must handle the freeform case, not panic on an unknown enum.

examples.title: Convert a session into a validated context
examples.intent: Promote raw collected answers into a context the loop can trust.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: session_to_context turns the raw InterviewSession (optional fields) into an InterviewContext carrying the task and validated fields; the loop consumes a coherent, task-bound context rather than loose answers.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Pinch the session node to consolidate its scattered answers into a single context card.
touch_interaction.visual: Loose answer chips draw together into one bound InterviewContext card stamped with the task.

examples.mini_scenario: session_to_context folds the answers plus the original task into one InterviewContext the planner reads.
examples.pitfall: The context binds the task alongside the answers — dropping the task on conversion strips the answers of what they scope.

examples.title: Infer scope for script-like tasks
examples.intent: Pre-answer scope when the task obviously implies a small script.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: infer_scope_default returns 'a' (Quick) when TaskHints.suggests_script, else None; the loop's budget starts small for throwaway scripts without asking.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press the scope node to see why Quick was pre-selected for a script task.
touch_interaction.visual: The Quick notch is pre-lit with a 'script detected' tag explaining the inference.

examples.mini_scenario: The task 'write a quick script to rename files' pre-selects Quick scope, so the loop budgets for a short run.
examples.pitfall: Inference returns None when unsure — don't fabricate a scope default; an absent default correctly leaves the question open.

examples.title: Skip framework for script or unknown language
examples.intent: Avoid asking for a framework where none applies.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: The framework question is skipped when the task suggests a script or no language is known; the loop scopes without a meaningless framework choice.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Flick past the framework node when the task is a bare script.
touch_interaction.visual: The framework node collapses with a 'not applicable' badge and no options shown.

examples.mini_scenario: The task is a shell one-liner script; the framework question is skipped entirely and the loop proceeds.
examples.pitfall: Skipping framework is correct for scripts — don't force a framework onto a task that has no framework concept.

examples.title: Accumulate extra notes as freeform scope
examples.intent: Let the operator add constraints the fixed questions don't cover.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: InterviewSession.extra_notes (Vec<String>) collects freeform lines; these flow into the system prompt so the loop honors constraints outside the standard question set.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Draw a line from a sticky-note bubble to the interview node to append an extra note.
touch_interaction.visual: Each note appears as a stacked sticky chip on the interview node, order preserved.

examples.mini_scenario: The operator adds 'must be dependency-free'; the note lands in extra_notes and constrains the loop's plan.
examples.pitfall: Extra notes are unstructured — the loop must actually read them; treating them as decoration lets real constraints slip.

examples.title: Infer project type from task signals
examples.intent: Pre-select the likely project type to shorten the questionnaire.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: infer_project_type_default returns a char key from TaskHints ('b' web_api, 'a' cli, 'c' frontend, 'd' library, 'f' script); the loop pre-fills the type question, needing only confirmation.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Long-press the type node to see which task signal chose the default key.
touch_interaction.visual: The inferred type chip is pre-lit with the matching signal name shown beneath it.

examples.mini_scenario: The task mentions 'CLI tool'; infer_project_type_default returns 'a' and pre-selects CliTool for confirmation.
examples.pitfall: The inference maps to a char key, not a final enum — the operator's confirmation still runs through parse_project_type.

examples.title: Distinguish TypeScript from JavaScript on detection
examples.intent: Detect the exact language variant so the plan targets the right toolchain.
examples.how_it_shapes_the_loop: detect_existing_project checks tsconfig.json vs package.json alone to tell TypeScript from JavaScript (and pyproject.toml/setup.py/requirements.txt for Python); the loop scopes to the precise ecosystem.

touch_interaction.canvas_action: Double-tap the detected-language chip to see which marker file resolved the variant.
touch_interaction.visual: The chip shows 'TypeScript' with a tsconfig.json footnote, distinct from a plain package.json JS detection.

examples.mini_scenario: The cwd has both package.json and tsconfig.json; detection reports TypeScript, so the plan targets ts tooling.
examples.pitfall: A package.json without tsconfig.json is JavaScript, not TypeScript — conflating them scopes the loop to the wrong toolchain.
